screens.title: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP) Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore EIGRP, a Cisco-developed routing protocol that blends Distance Vector simplicity with Link-State intelligence. You will learn why EIGRP is often chosen over older protocols like RIP: it converges faster, uses partial updates to save bandwidth, and relies on the Diffusing Update Algorithm to prevent routing loops. We'll look at the key concepts you need: how DUAL uses a topology table and two distances — Advertised Distance and Feasible Distance — to select primary and backup paths; how feasible successors enable near-instant failover; the five EIGRP packet types used for neighbor discovery and reliable updates; the adjacency criteria routers must meet before exchanging routes; and the composite metric made primarily from Bandwidth and Delay. A practical topology exercise is included so you can configure two routers, observe neighbors and the topology table, and test failover. By the end you should be able to explain how EIGRP guarantees loop-free alternate paths, why partial updates matter for efficiency, and how to spot common misconfigurations. Consider how fast failover and efficient updates would affect application availability in an enterprise network. What difference would near-instant route recovery make for a voice or database application?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives guide our study of EIGRP fundamentals. First, you will describe EIGRP as an advanced Distance Vector protocol and contrast it with RIP. That means explaining partial updates, faster convergence, and why EIGRP scales better. Second, you will explain the role of the Diffusing Update Algorithm, or DUAL, which maintains a topology table and enforces the Feasibility Condition so routers can choose loop-free backup paths. Third, you will identify the five EIGRP packet types — Hello, Update, Query, Reply, and ACK — and explain each packet's role in neighbor formation and reliable routing exchanges. Finally, you will define and calculate the EIGRP metric: know how Bandwidth and Delay combine by default, what K-values mean, and why Reliability and Load are seldom used. Each objective includes a practical angle: describe a troubleshooting step, interpret topology outputs, or compute a metric for two links. Together these objectives let you configure EIGRP, verify neighbors and topology entries, and reason about route selection and failures in an enterprise environment. As you study, ask yourself how each objective maps to real evidence on the router: which show commands will prove your understanding?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Evidence
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond conceptual knowledge, you will practice three concrete verification skills. First, configure EIGRP on two routers with the same Autonomous System and confirm neighbors with the show ip eigrp neighbors command. Seeing a neighbor entry with hold time and uptime is evidence that Hello packets and adjacency criteria were met. Second, inspect the topology table using show ip eigrp topology to find Successor and Feasible Successor entries, noting Advertised and Feasible Distances. This lets you confirm DUAL decisions and the Feasibility Condition. Third, compute and compare the metric in the routing table using show ip route eigrp; match the displayed metric to your manual calculation based on bandwidth and cumulative delay. These hands-on checks are practical proofs of understanding: they show that the router is using the same K-values, that interfaces share a primary subnet, and that partial updates are flowing. As you practice, watch for common mismatches — for example, incorrect network statements or different AS numbers — and treat them as troubleshooting leads. Each verification maps directly to an objective and provides observable evidence you can use during operations or assessments.

screens.title: EIGRP vs RIP — Why EIGRP improves on RIP
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP and RIP are both distance-vector family members historically, but they behave differently in ways that matter for enterprise networks. RIP sends full routing updates periodically, which can consume bandwidth and delay convergence on large networks. EIGRP, by contrast, sends partial, bounded updates only when topology changes occur. This saves bandwidth and reduces noisy chatter across links. Another crucial difference is convergence speed. RIP relies on timers and incremental updates that can be slow to react to failures; EIGRP uses DUAL to compute loop-free backup paths ahead of time when possible, enabling near-instant failover to a feasible successor. That difference affects application availability — voice or database traffic hurt by even short route flaps will benefit from EIGRP’s faster reconvergence. A common misconception is that EIGRP is simply a faster RIP; it's not. EIGRP maintains a topology table with more information, uses composite metrics instead of hop count, and has reliable delivery mechanisms for updates, queries, and replies. For troubleshooting, ask whether periodic timers or inefficient updates are the root cause; if so, RIP’s behavior is probably to blame. In short, EIGRP preserves the simplicity of distance-vector design while adding smarter path computation and efficient updates, making it a stronger choice for larger or performance-sensitive networks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › EIGRP vs RIP
EIGRP vs RIP
Key operational differences
RIP — Classic Distance Vector
  • Periodic full routing table updates.
  • Hop count metric, limited scalability.
  • Slower convergence due to timers and updates.
Common issue: bandwidth used by periodic full updates on large networks.
EIGRP — Advanced Distance Vector
  • Partial, event-driven updates reduce bandwidth use.
  • DUAL ensures loop-free paths and enables feasible successors.
  • Composite metric (bandwidth and delay) improves path quality.
Advantage: faster reconvergence and better scalability.
Why it matters
Faster failover reduces application downtime and improves user experience.
Misconception
EIGRP is not just a faster RIP; it changes how updates and path computation work.
Check
Ask: is the network using partial updates and does the topology table show feasible successors?

screens.title: DUAL and the topology table
screens.narratorSegment: DUAL, the Diffusing Update Algorithm, is the engine that gives EIGRP its reliability. At its core, DUAL keeps a topology table that records every route the router learns from neighbors, not just the route selected for the routing table. Each topology entry includes attributes such as Advertised Distance, which is the neighbor’s reported metric to a destination, and the local Feasible Distance, which is the best known metric from this router to the destination. DUAL uses those values to determine the Successor — the next-hop with the lowest Feasible Distance — and to identify Feasible Successors that satisfy the Feasibility Condition. The Feasibility Condition requires that a neighbor’s Advertised Distance is strictly less than the current Feasible Distance; when that holds, the neighbor is guaranteed to provide a loop-free alternate. The topology table therefore acts like a ledger of possible paths so that when a link fails, the router can check for eligible alternates without immediately querying neighbors. A common misconception is that only the routing table matters. In EIGRP, observing the topology table is essential during troubleshooting because it shows backup paths and the FD/AD values you use to verify loop prevention. Understanding the topology table and DUAL’s decision rules is central to predicting EIGRP behavior during failures.

keyIdea.title: DUAL takeaway
keyIdea.text: DUAL's topology table holds FD and AD values so the router can pick successors and feasible successors that guarantee loop-free alternates.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › DUAL & Topology Table
Topology Table — what it stores
  • Routes learned from each neighbor with their Advertised Distance (AD).
  • Local Feasible Distance (FD) values for each destination.
  • Candidate successors and feasible successors.
Why this matters: the topology table preserves multiple candidate paths so DUAL can choose safe alternates without immediate neighbor queries when possible.
Architecture: FD vs AD
Advertised Distance (AD): the metric a neighbor advertises for the destination. Feasible Distance (FD): the router’s best calculated metric to the destination, including cost to reach that neighbor plus the neighbor’s AD.
Example
If neighbor N reports AD 2000 and your cost to N is 500, your candidate path has FD=2500. If FD currently is 3000, N is a feasible successor because 2000 < 3000.
Tip: use show ip eigrp topology to inspect AD and FD values directly during troubleshooting.

screens.title: Selecting Successors and Feasible Successors
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting a primary and backup path in EIGRP follows a clear process rooted in the Feasibility Condition. First, the router examines topology entries and computes the Feasible Distance for each candidate path by adding the local cost to reach the neighbor and the neighbor’s Advertised Distance. The router then chooses the path with the lowest Feasible Distance as the Successor. Next, it looks at other neighbors as potential Feasible Successors: a neighbor qualifies if its Advertised Distance is strictly less than the current Feasible Distance. That inequality is the Feasibility Condition and it mathematically guarantees the alternate path is loop-free. If a Successor fails and at least one Feasible Successor exists, the router swaps to the backup route almost instantly, avoiding the delay and traffic of queries. If no Feasible Successor exists, the route moves to an active state and the router sends reliable Query packets to neighbors to discover alternative paths, which can be resource intensive. A misconception is assuming any neighbor with a low metric is automatically loop-free; only when the Advertised Distance meets the Feasibility Condition can you trust the neighbor as a safe alternate. Practice: compute FD and AD from the topology table and predict whether a given neighbor will be a feasible successor before testing failure scenarios.

keyIdea.title: Failover principle
keyIdea.text: A feasible successor meets AD < FD; if present, it enables immediate loop-free failover without queries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Successor Selection
Selection Steps
  1. Compute FD by adding cost to neighbor plus neighbor's AD.
  2. Select Successor: lowest FD becomes the primary route.
  3. Find Feasible Successors: neighbors where AD < current FD.
  4. If Successor fails, use Feasible Successor if available; otherwise enter active state and send Queries.
Key Takeaway
Feasible successors let EIGRP fail over immediately and safely without neighbor queries.
Concrete Example
Current FD to network X = 3000. Neighbor A advertises AD=2000 and cost to reach A is 500; candidate FD=2500, and since 2000 < 3000, A is a feasible successor. If the primary fails, switch to A immediately.
Misconception: low AD alone doesn't prove safety; it must be less than the current FD to satisfy feasibility.

screens.title: EIGRP packet types and their roles
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP uses five packet types to handle discovery, reliable updates, and queries. Hello packets are the discovery mechanism: sent periodically to identify neighbors and maintain adjacency with information such as AS number, K-values, and hold time. They are the heartbeat that keeps neighbor relationships alive. Update packets carry routing information — new routes or changes — and are sent reliably to specific neighbors; they require acknowledgment. Query packets are used only when a router loses its primary route and has no feasible successor; they are reliable and ask neighbors for alternative paths. Reply packets answer those Queries, indicating whether the neighbor has a route to the requested destination; Replies are also reliable. Finally, ACK packets acknowledge receipt of reliable packets like Update, Query, and Reply; they may be implemented as unicast Hello packets with an acknowledgment number. A useful contrast: Hello packets are periodic and unordered, while Update, Query, and Reply are reliably delivered and must be acknowledged to ensure consistent state across routers. When troubleshooting, missing neighbors often trace back to blocked Hello packets or mismatched AS numbers or K-values. Understanding each packet type clarifies why some messages are retransmitted and why EIGRP scales reliability without flooding the network with full-table transfers.

keyIdea.text: Hello discovers neighbors; Update, Query, and Reply exchange reliable routing state; ACK confirms reliable delivery.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › EIGRP Packets
Hello
Discovers neighbors, shares AS and K-values, and maintains adjacency. Sent periodically: default timers vary by link speed.
Update
Carries route information reliably to specific neighbors; requires acknowledgment.
Query
Sent when no feasible successor exists to ask neighbors for alternate paths; reliable and potentially resource intensive.
Reply
Response to a Query indicating whether the neighbor has the requested route; reliable.
ACK
Acknowledges receipt of reliable EIGRP packets. Often implemented as a unicast Hello with an acknowledgment number.
Pro tip: when Queries and Replies spike, review topology stability and check for missing feasible successors to reduce active-state messaging.

screens.title: EIGRP adjacency criteria
screens.narratorSegment: Routers must meet several precise criteria to become EIGRP neighbors and form adjacencies. First, they must belong to the same EIGRP Autonomous System number; differing AS numbers prevent adjacency because routers treat routes from other ASes as external. Second, their interfaces must be on the same primary subnet so Hello packets can be received at the IP layer. Third, K-values — the metric weights used by EIGRP — must match between neighbors. If routers use different K-values they calculate metrics differently, leading to inconsistent routing decisions, so adjacency will not form. Fourth, if authentication is configured, the neighbors must pass it; mismatched keys or methods block adjacency. Finally, routers should have unique Router IDs; while not strictly required for adjacency in all cases, ID conflicts can cause operational confusion and should be avoided. A common troubleshooting path is to validate these criteria using configuration and show commands: check AS numbers in router configuration, confirm interface IPs share the same subnet, verify K-values or that defaults are in use, and inspect authentication settings. Remember: adjacency depends on agreement across these parameters, and resolving mismatches often restores neighbor relationships quickly.

keyIdea.title: Adjacency checklist
keyIdea.text: Match AS number, primary subnet, and K-values; pass authentication; and ensure unique Router IDs to form EIGRP neighbors.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Adjacency Criteria
Adjacency Requirements
  • Same EIGRP Autonomous System number.
  • Interfaces on the same primary subnet so Hello packets are exchanged.
  • Matching K-values (metric weights).
  • Authentication succeeds if configured on either side.
  • Unique Router IDs to avoid identification conflicts.
Troubleshoot
Check show ip eigrp neighbors output and compare configured AS and K-values on both routers.
Misconception
Router ID conflicts alone rarely block adjacency formation, but they can cause operational confusion and must be unique.

screens.title: EIGRP metric components
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP uses a composite metric composed of multiple components; by default only Bandwidth and Delay are used. Bandwidth is the minimum link bandwidth along the path and is expressed in kilobits per second; the slowest link dominates the bandwidth component of the metric. Delay is the cumulative interface delay along the path, measured in tens of microseconds at the interface level. Reliability and Load exist as optional inputs but are rarely used because they change dynamically and can cause frequent metric recalculation and route instability. Reliability is a measure of error-free transmission over an interface; Load reflects current utilization. K-values control which components are included in the composite metric: with default K1=1 and K3=1, and K2=K4=K5=0, the formula simplifies and relies on bandwidth and delay only. When designing or troubleshooting EIGRP, focus first on bandwidth and delay because they are the typical drivers of path selection. A common misconception is to assume more dynamic metrics like Load should be enabled to prefer lightly loaded links; in practice, using Load or Reliability can introduce instability as values fluctuate. Understand the trade-off: simplicity and predictability with defaults versus dynamic responsiveness with additional components, and prefer defaults in most enterprise deployments.

keyIdea.title: Metric focus
keyIdea.text: By default EIGRP uses Bandwidth and Delay; Reliability and Load are optional but can cause instability if used routinely.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › EIGRP Metric Components
Bandwidth
The minimum link bandwidth in kbps along the path. It is used to represent the slowest hop's capacity and strongly influences the metric.
Delay
The sum of interface delays in tens of microseconds along the path; combined with bandwidth to form the default metric.
Reliability
Optional; a measure of error-free operation. Rarely used because it is dynamic and can cause instability.
Load
Optional; current utilization. Also dynamic and not commonly included in enterprise metric calculations.
Default K-values
K1 = 1, K3 = 1, K2 = K4 = K5 = 0 — which simplifies the metric to use Bandwidth and Delay only.

screens.title: EIGRP metric formula and worked example
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP's general metric formula includes weighted contributions from Bandwidth, Delay, Reliability, and Load. Expressed with K-values, the full formula multiplies a composite sum by a reliability factor. However, most deployments use default K-values where K1 and K3 are one and K2, K4, K5 are zero. With those defaults the formula simplifies to a familiar form: Metric = (10^7 / Bandwidth) + Delay. Bandwidth is the minimum interface bandwidth in kilobits per second along the path; Delay is the sum of interface delays in tens of microseconds. Let's work through an example. Suppose a path's slowest link has bandwidth 1000 kbps and cumulative delay equals 2000 (in the units EIGRP uses). The bandwidth component becomes 10^7 divided by 1000, which is 10000. Add the Delay of 2000 to get a metric of 12000. This numeric result is what EIGRP uses to compare paths: lower is better. A typical troubleshooting error is to forget the units or to sum delays incorrectly; always use the router's interface delay values and confirm the link bandwidth used is the minimum along the path. Practice computing metrics for alternate paths and check them against show ip route eigrp outputs to verify the router's selection.

keyIdea.text: With default K-values, EIGRP metric is Metric = (10^7 / Bandwidth) + Delay; lower values indicate better paths.

content.html:

General formula
Metric = [K1 * Bandwidth + (K2 * Bandwidth) / (256 - Load) + K3 * Delay] * [K5 / (Reliability + K4)]
Default K-values simplify this expression in typical deployments.
Default simplified formula
Metric = (10^7 / Bandwidth) + Delay
Worked example: Bandwidth=1000 kbps, Delay=2000 → 10^7 / 1000 = 10000; 10000 + 2000 = 12000 metric.
Practice
Compute metrics for two alternative paths and predict which EIGRP will prefer based on the lower metric.
Misconception
Do not forget units: bandwidth in kbps and delay in tens of microseconds are required for correct calculations.

screens.title: Partial updates, active state, and convergence
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP reduces bandwidth usage by sending partial, bounded updates rather than full-table periodic broadcasts. When a route changes, routers advertise only the changed information to affected neighbors. This event-driven behavior keeps the network quieter and scales better than periodic full-table updates. However, there are times when EIGRP must escalate: if a route is lost and no feasible successor exists, the router sets the route to an active state and sends reliable Query packets to its neighbors asking for alternative paths. These Queries and the corresponding Replies can be resource intensive because they require the neighbors to search their topology and possibly propagate queries further. Thus network stability and appropriate design are important: keeping feasible successors available avoids active states and reduces query storms. A common operational pitfall is misinterpreting query traffic as a protocol storm; in many cases it is symptomatic of missing feasible successors or frequent topology flaps. When debugging convergence issues, check whether feasible successors exist in the topology table and whether changes occur rapidly enough to cause active-state behavior. Ultimately, EIGRP offers efficient normal operation but requires stable topology or planning for backup paths to prevent expensive query resolutions.

screens.title: Common mistakes and operational tips
screens.narratorSegment: When operating EIGRP, a few recurring issues account for most neighbor or path selection problems. First, mismatched Autonomous System numbers are an immediate adjacency blocker; always confirm the AS configured under router eigrp matches across neighbors. Second, K-value mismatches prevent adjacency because routers compute metrics differently; ensure K-values are the same or default on both sides. Third, wrong network statements or incorrect interface addressing can place routers on different subnets so Hello packets never arrive — this is a common configuration mistake. Fourth, authentication misconfiguration results in neighbor rejection; verify keys and algorithms if auth is used. Fifth, expecting dynamic metrics like Load to stabilize is risky; enabling Load or Reliability can trigger frequent recalculation and instability. Operational tips: prefer the default K-values in production, verify topology table entries rather than only the routing table when troubleshooting, and plan for feasible successors in design to avoid active states during failures. If you see query storms, check for rapid topology changes or missing feasible successors. These steps cover the typical root causes and will get most EIGRP issues resolved quickly. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore EIGRP, a Cisco-developed routing protocol that blends Distance Vector simplicity with Link-State intelligence. You will learn why EIGRP is often chosen over older protocols like RIP: it converges faster, uses partial updates to save bandwidth, and relies on the Diffusing Update Algorithm to prevent routing loops. We'll look at the key concepts you need: how DUAL uses a topology table and two distances — Advertised Distance and Feasible Distance — to select primary and backup paths; how feasible successors enable near-instant failover; the five EIGRP packet types used for neighbor discovery and reliable updates; the adjacency criteria routers must meet before exchanging routes; and the composite metric made primarily from Bandwidth and Delay. A practical topology exercise is included so you can configure two routers, observe neighbors and the topology table, and test failover. By the end you should be able to explain how EIGRP guarantees loop-free alternate paths, why partial updates matter for efficiency, and how to spot common misconfigurations. Consider how fast failover and efficient updates would affect application availability in an enterprise network. What difference would near-instant route recovery make for a voice or database application?

These four objectives guide our study of EIGRP fundamentals. First, you will describe EIGRP as an advanced Distance Vector protocol and contrast it with RIP. That means explaining partial updates, faster convergence, and why EIGRP scales better. Second, you will explain the role of the Diffusing Update Algorithm, or DUAL, which maintains a topology table and enforces the Feasibility Condition so routers can choose loop-free backup paths. Third, you will identify the five EIGRP packet types — Hello, Update, Query, Reply, and ACK — and explain each packet's role in neighbor formation and reliable routing exchanges. Finally, you will define and calculate the EIGRP metric: know how Bandwidth and Delay combine by default, what K-values mean, and why Reliability and Load are seldom used. Each objective includes a practical angle: describe a troubleshooting step, interpret topology outputs, or compute a metric for two links. Together these objectives let you configure EIGRP, verify neighbors and topology entries, and reason about route selection and failures in an enterprise environment. As you study, ask yourself how each objective maps to real evidence on the router: which show commands will prove your understanding?

Beyond conceptual knowledge, you will practice three concrete verification skills. First, configure EIGRP on two routers with the same Autonomous System and confirm neighbors with the show ip eigrp neighbors command. Seeing a neighbor entry with hold time and uptime is evidence that Hello packets and adjacency criteria were met. Second, inspect the topology table using show ip eigrp topology to find Successor and Feasible Successor entries, noting Advertised and Feasible Distances. This lets you confirm DUAL decisions and the Feasibility Condition. Third, compute and compare the metric in the routing table using show ip route eigrp; match the displayed metric to your manual calculation based on bandwidth and cumulative delay. These hands-on checks are practical proofs of understanding: they show that the router is using the same K-values, that interfaces share a primary subnet, and that partial updates are flowing. As you practice, watch for common mismatches — for example, incorrect network statements or different AS numbers — and treat them as troubleshooting leads. Each verification maps directly to an objective and provides observable evidence you can use during operations or assessments.

EIGRP and RIP are both distance-vector family members historically, but they behave differently in ways that matter for enterprise networks. RIP sends full routing updates periodically, which can consume bandwidth and delay convergence on large networks. EIGRP, by contrast, sends partial, bounded updates only when topology changes occur. This saves bandwidth and reduces noisy chatter across links. Another crucial difference is convergence speed. RIP relies on timers and incremental updates that can be slow to react to failures; EIGRP uses DUAL to compute loop-free backup paths ahead of time when possible, enabling near-instant failover to a feasible successor. That difference affects application availability — voice or database traffic hurt by even short route flaps will benefit from EIGRP’s faster reconvergence. A common misconception is that EIGRP is simply a faster RIP; it's not. EIGRP maintains a topology table with more information, uses composite metrics instead of hop count, and has reliable delivery mechanisms for updates, queries, and replies. For troubleshooting, ask whether periodic timers or inefficient updates are the root cause; if so, RIP’s behavior is probably to blame. In short, EIGRP preserves the simplicity of distance-vector design while adding smarter path computation and efficient updates, making it a stronger choice for larger or performance-sensitive networks.

DUAL, the Diffusing Update Algorithm, is the engine that gives EIGRP its reliability. At its core, DUAL keeps a topology table that records every route the router learns from neighbors, not just the route selected for the routing table. Each topology entry includes attributes such as Advertised Distance, which is the neighbor’s reported metric to a destination, and the local Feasible Distance, which is the best known metric from this router to the destination. DUAL uses those values to determine the Successor — the next-hop with the lowest Feasible Distance — and to identify Feasible Successors that satisfy the Feasibility Condition. The Feasibility Condition requires that a neighbor’s Advertised Distance is strictly less than the current Feasible Distance; when that holds, the neighbor is guaranteed to provide a loop-free alternate. The topology table therefore acts like a ledger of possible paths so that when a link fails, the router can check for eligible alternates without immediately querying neighbors. A common misconception is that only the routing table matters. In EIGRP, observing the topology table is essential during troubleshooting because it shows backup paths and the FD/AD values you use to verify loop prevention. Understanding the topology table and DUAL’s decision rules is central to predicting EIGRP behavior during failures.

Selecting a primary and backup path in EIGRP follows a clear process rooted in the Feasibility Condition. First, the router examines topology entries and computes the Feasible Distance for each candidate path by adding the local cost to reach the neighbor and the neighbor’s Advertised Distance. The router then chooses the path with the lowest Feasible Distance as the Successor. Next, it looks at other neighbors as potential Feasible Successors: a neighbor qualifies if its Advertised Distance is strictly less than the current Feasible Distance. That inequality is the Feasibility Condition and it mathematically guarantees the alternate path is loop-free. If a Successor fails and at least one Feasible Successor exists, the router swaps to the backup route almost instantly, avoiding the delay and traffic of queries. If no Feasible Successor exists, the route moves to an active state and the router sends reliable Query packets to neighbors to discover alternative paths, which can be resource intensive. A misconception is assuming any neighbor with a low metric is automatically loop-free; only when the Advertised Distance meets the Feasibility Condition can you trust the neighbor as a safe alternate. Practice: compute FD and AD from the topology table and predict whether a given neighbor will be a feasible successor before testing failure scenarios.

EIGRP uses five packet types to handle discovery, reliable updates, and queries. Hello packets are the discovery mechanism: sent periodically to identify neighbors and maintain adjacency with information such as AS number, K-values, and hold time. They are the heartbeat that keeps neighbor relationships alive. Update packets carry routing information — new routes or changes — and are sent reliably to specific neighbors; they require acknowledgment. Query packets are used only when a router loses its primary route and has no feasible successor; they are reliable and ask neighbors for alternative paths. Reply packets answer those Queries, indicating whether the neighbor has a route to the requested destination; Replies are also reliable. Finally, ACK packets acknowledge receipt of reliable packets like Update, Query, and Reply; they may be implemented as unicast Hello packets with an acknowledgment number. A useful contrast: Hello packets are periodic and unordered, while Update, Query, and Reply are reliably delivered and must be acknowledged to ensure consistent state across routers. When troubleshooting, missing neighbors often trace back to blocked Hello packets or mismatched AS numbers or K-values. Understanding each packet type clarifies why some messages are retransmitted and why EIGRP scales reliability without flooding the network with full-table transfers.

Routers must meet several precise criteria to become EIGRP neighbors and form adjacencies. First, they must belong to the same EIGRP Autonomous System number; differing AS numbers prevent adjacency because routers treat routes from other ASes as external. Second, their interfaces must be on the same primary subnet so Hello packets can be received at the IP layer. Third, K-values — the metric weights used by EIGRP — must match between neighbors. If routers use different K-values they calculate metrics differently, leading to inconsistent routing decisions, so adjacency will not form. Fourth, if authentication is configured, the neighbors must pass it; mismatched keys or methods block adjacency. Finally, routers should have unique Router IDs; while not strictly required for adjacency in all cases, ID conflicts can cause operational confusion and should be avoided. A common troubleshooting path is to validate these criteria using configuration and show commands: check AS numbers in router configuration, confirm interface IPs share the same subnet, verify K-values or that defaults are in use, and inspect authentication settings. Remember: adjacency depends on agreement across these parameters, and resolving mismatches often restores neighbor relationships quickly.

EIGRP uses a composite metric composed of multiple components; by default only Bandwidth and Delay are used. Bandwidth is the minimum link bandwidth along the path and is expressed in kilobits per second; the slowest link dominates the bandwidth component of the metric. Delay is the cumulative interface delay along the path, measured in tens of microseconds at the interface level. Reliability and Load exist as optional inputs but are rarely used because they change dynamically and can cause frequent metric recalculation and route instability. Reliability is a measure of error-free transmission over an interface; Load reflects current utilization. K-values control which components are included in the composite metric: with default K1=1 and K3=1, and K2=K4=K5=0, the formula simplifies and relies on bandwidth and delay only. When designing or troubleshooting EIGRP, focus first on bandwidth and delay because they are the typical drivers of path selection. A common misconception is to assume more dynamic metrics like Load should be enabled to prefer lightly loaded links; in practice, using Load or Reliability can introduce instability as values fluctuate. Understand the trade-off: simplicity and predictability with defaults versus dynamic responsiveness with additional components, and prefer defaults in most enterprise deployments.

EIGRP's general metric formula includes weighted contributions from Bandwidth, Delay, Reliability, and Load. Expressed with K-values, the full formula multiplies a composite sum by a reliability factor. However, most deployments use default K-values where K1 and K3 are one and K2, K4, K5 are zero. With those defaults the formula simplifies to a familiar form: Metric = (10^7 / Bandwidth) + Delay. Bandwidth is the minimum interface bandwidth in kilobits per second along the path; Delay is the sum of interface delays in tens of microseconds. Let's work through an example. Suppose a path's slowest link has bandwidth 1000 kbps and cumulative delay equals 2000 (in the units EIGRP uses). The bandwidth component becomes 10^7 divided by 1000, which is 10000. Add the Delay of 2000 to get a metric of 12000. This numeric result is what EIGRP uses to compare paths: lower is better. A typical troubleshooting error is to forget the units or to sum delays incorrectly; always use the router's interface delay values and confirm the link bandwidth used is the minimum along the path. Practice computing metrics for alternate paths and check them against show ip route eigrp outputs to verify the router's selection.

When debugging convergence issues, check whether feasible successors exist in the topology table and whether changes occur rapidly enough to cause active-state behavior. Ultimately, EIGRP offers efficient normal operation but requires stable topology or planning for backup paths to prevent expensive query resolutions.
